# Remote Recruitment to Diversify Infant Research Participation: Lessons From the Infant Vaccine Biepository

**Authors:** Eleanor Nicholson; Ritobhas Bhowmik; Emily Stonestreet; Ganad Neka; Audrey Mutoni; Amanda Michael; Tina Yi Jin Hsieh; McKenzi Thompson; Valerie Perrinez; Alejandra Barrero-Castillero; Ai-ris Y. Collier

**Affiliations:** 1Center for Virology and Vaccine Research, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 2Department of Obstetrics, Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 3Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 4Department of Neonatology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

To determine whether remote recruitment, electronic consent and at-home blood collection enabled enrollment of a geographically and socioeconomically diverse infant cohort in the United States (US).

We describe the demographics of 256 infants included in this analysis, drawn from 264 enrolled in the Infant Vaccine Biorepository (December 2022–April 2026). Participants were recruited via online advertising and electronic medical record messaging. Geographic distribution was assessed using US Census regions and Rural–Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) codes. Social vulnerability was characterized using the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) at census tract and county levels, with nationwide rankings.

Infants were distributed evenly across the four US geographic regions; 9% resided in rural areas. Based on nationwide census tract-level SVI rankings, 39.8% of participants fell in the medium-high or high vulnerability categories. County-level SVI rankings indicated that 57.0% of participants fell in these same categories. Participants were 78% White and 20% Hispanic; 94.1% of mothers had received at least one COVID-19 vaccine.

Fully remote recruitment, consent and specimen collection enabled enrollment of infants from diverse geographic and socioeconomic backgrounds across the US. SVI and RUCA provide richer characterization of study populations than traditional demographic measures alone.

## Introduction

Research study populations often fail to represent target communities. Historically, women and minorities are underrepresented, and pregnant women are often excluded without justification [1]. Low-income individuals and those living in rural areas are also less likely to participate [2]. Although there has been a push to improve the diversity of clinical trials, drug trial enrollment still does not represent the United States (US) population. In 2024, participants across all trials were 70% White, 17% Asian, 8% Black, 19% Hispanic, and 5% American Indian/Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, Other, Unknown/Unreported [3]. White participants remain overrepresented, while Black participants remain underrepresented. Many clinical trials lack adequate demographic information that captures socioeconomic status. Multiple longitudinal studies have found that less than half of US-based clinical trials report race and ethnicity, let alone socioeconomic information, of which less than 15% of studies report [4, 5].

Clinical research site location limits geographic representation. Traditionally, clinical trials and observational studies are conducted at urban academic research centers. In 2020, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) reported that 50% of clinical drug trials took place in 1%–2% of zip codes [6]. Recruitment practices are often centered in academic institutions, which can be harder for some communities to access—thereby reducing the fairness of clinical trials [7, 8]. In vaccine research, this limitation is especially problematic because vaccine uptake could be lower and infections may have a greater burden in communities that might not be included as research participants [9]. Without adequate representation, generalizability of the results and the perceived efficacy of the data may both be reduced, and this may impact public trust of clinical trials and treatment options [10]. As a result, inequities may worsen because the standard of care is based on incomplete evidence.

Most clinical studies report race and ethnicity alone, which may not fully reflect the socioeconomic factors that shape health outcomes. United States mailing addresses can be utilized to determine the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) of the area where our study participants reside. SVI was developed by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to help identify communities particularly vulnerable to public health emergencies and disasters [11]. The measure includes four overarching domains: socioeconomic status, household characteristics, racial and ethnic minority status and housing type and transportation. Each domain contains specific subgroups such as health insurance status, education level, proficiency in English, or whether it is a single-parent household. Individuals living in high-SVI areas may reside farther from large academic research centers, and may also have lower income and face more significant barriers to in-person research, such as travel time, transportation costs and unpaid time off work [2, 12]. Individuals living in higher SVI areas are at higher risk for infectious diseases, and those populations may experience more difficulty in accessing clinical studies [9]. Another tool that can be used to assess a participant’s experience and level of accessibility to clinical trials are Rural–Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) codes [13]. These codes were developed by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) to understand how rural or urban a census tract was based on commuting patterns to and from that area. Generally, RUCA codes 1–3 are defined as urban and 4–10 as rural. Researchers have leveraged RUCA to understand disparities in access to healthcare and how rurality may affect patient outcomes in clinical trials [14, 15]. One retrospective study exploring patient access to clinical trials in the rural Northwestern US found that participants were mostly from metropolitan areas as defined by RUCA, though 22% of participants were from rural areas [16]. Their conclusion was that as trials become more decentralized and offer more remote options, representation of rural populations will increase and improve the generalizability of trial results [16]. Our study’s use of remote recruitment, informed consent, data and specimen collection may mitigate barriers to research participation by reducing cost burdens and increasing representation by the communities most affected.

The Infant Vaccine Biorepository began in 2022 at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC). Initially, this study began at a single urban hospital and recruitment occurred in person; however, in identifying the need for diverse participant participation, the study quickly expanded across the US with the help of an online recruitment platform, electronic informed consent and remote capillary blood collection. The goal of the Infant Vaccine Biorepository protocol is to understand the magnitude and durability of passive immunity transferred from birthing parent to infant via the placenta by enrolling representative infants across the United States. This protocol was developed to reduce socioeconomic and geographic barriers to participation through a remote recruitment, consent and blood collection processes. The objective of this analysis is to characterize the geographic and socioeconomic diversity of our de-centralized research cohort using RUCA codes and SVI, which better capture infectious disease and health risk contexts than traditional demographic measures.

## Methods

### Study Population and Protocol

The study cohort includes infants enrolled through the Infant Vaccine Biorepository protocol from December 2022 to April 2026. Written informed consent was obtained from the legally authorized representative (LAR) of the infant. The Institutional Review Board at BIDMC approved this study (BIDMC IRB#2022P000765). Infants actively on study are 3 through 12 months of age. The infant cohort was recruited remotely using OpenClinica (previously BuildClinical), a digital recruitment platform that targets online study advertisements to potentially eligible participants. Eligible participants were pregnant people or people with infants under 13 months of age. Written consent was obtained from participants by phone using a remote e-consent platform (REDCap). Parents and guardians consented on behalf of the infant and had the opportunity to consent themselves to enroll in the study, as well. Once the participants had consented, we collected demographics, infant feeding method, vaccine and infection history by self-report through an online questionnaire on REDCap. We also captured the medical history, obstetric information and vaccine and infection history of the birthing parent. Parents sent infant samples to us at three time points using the Tasso+ Blood Collection device at three timepoints: 3–5, 6–8 and 10–12 months of age [17]. Prior to each sample collection, study coordinators contacted the parent or guardian for updated infant vaccine and infection history. Participants were provided financial compensation for each sample collection using gift cards distributed electronically by email.

### Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) Calculation

Participants provided a mailing address as part of study participation for sending and returning sample collection kits. The mailing address was also used to calculate their SVI. SVI can be assessed in four ways based on two dimensions: geographic level and comparison scale. SVI may be calculated at either the county- or census tract-level and compared either nationwide or within a given state. Here, we report both county- and census tract-level SVI data using nationwide rankings, meaning values are compared across the entire United States rather than within individual states. Although SVI values can be obtained from the CDC’s website by entering individual addresses, this approach is inefficient for large cohorts. Accordingly, all addresses were batch-geocoded to efficiently generate the SVI data. We used the United States. Census geocoding application programming interface (API) through the censusxy package in RStudio (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria), the sf package for spatial processing and 2018 U.S. Census Bureau cartographic boundary shapefiles for all states represented in the study [18–21]. Street addresses were batch converted to latitude and longitude coordinates, spatially matched to census tracts and assigned corresponding Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) codes. Since FIPS codes can be linked to both county- and census tract-level SVI values, the FIPS codes we generated were merged with the CDC’s county- and census tract-level 2022 SVI datasets [22]. This process allowed us to assign SVI values to the whole study cohort included in the analysis.

### Rural–Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) Calculation

RUCA codes were developed by the USDA Economic Research Service to define the degree of urbanization and rurality of a census tract based on commuting patterns and size of nearby urban centers [13]. We utilized FIPS codes generated from the SVI calculation to assign each participant a RUCA code from the 2020 tract data. RUCA has a two-level classification system, with secondary RUCA codes incorporating additional commuting flow information. Secondary RUCA codes were not considered in this analysis. There are 10 primary RUCA codes, with 1–3 being Urban/Metropolitan and 4–10 being Rural/Nonmetropolitan. Primary level RUCA codes were assigned by linking census tracts with the tract-level 2020 RUCA dataset in R [13].

### Missing Data

Demographic information was obtained by self-report. Participants were allowed to decline response, and missing data from self-reports are reported as missing or unknown in Table 1.

Batch geocoding was unsuccessful for 66 addresses. These addresses were manually entered into the CDC SVI website to obtain SVI rankings. Census tracts may be split once their maximum populations are reached, which can result in changes to FIPS codes [23]. Because the cartographic boundary shapefiles used in this analysis were based on census information from 2018, whereas SVI values were taken from 2022 datasets, addresses located in census tracts that split between 2018 and 2022 could not be linked to SVI values if the original 2018 FIPS code was no longer valid. For example, a tract coded 7000 in 2018 may have been split into 7001 and 7002 by 2022 preventing direct linkage. In contrast, the CDC SVI website uses updated census tract boundaries that were not captured in the shapefiles used in this analysis, allowing linkage to current FIPS codes and corresponding SVI values. Also, 2 of the 256 geocoded addresses initially yielded unknown RUCA codes (i.e., neither urban nor rural). The corresponding FIPS codes were not present in the 2020 tract-level RUCA dataset likely because the census tracts split after 2020, and updated tract-level RUCA files were not available. We were able to designate the addresses as Urban or Rural using a ZIP code-based RUCA lookup tool; however, ZIP codes are less specific than census tracts [24]. Using the above techniques, we were able to interpolate all SVI rankings and RUCA codes for our cohort.

### Statistical Analysis

Descriptive statistics were used to report infant demographic information (Table 1). Continuous variables were summarized using the median and interquartile range (IQR) and categorical variables were summarized as frequencies and percentages. Participants were categorized into 4 US regions according to Table S1. Rural versus urban residence was classified using 2020 RUCA codes linked to participant census tracts and reported in two categories with RUCA 1–3 assigned Urban/Metropolitan and 4–10 assigned. Demographic summary tables were generated in R. We report the proportion of participants in each SVI quartile as frequencies and percentages, with the least vulnerable in the lowest quartile and the most vulnerable in the highest quartile (Table 2). Vaccination status was summarized as number/total and percent, with maternal vaccination categorized as any maternal vaccine during pregnancy versus none, infant vaccination categorized as any reported infant vaccine versus none, and COVID-19 vaccination status summarized separately for the parent (Table 3). Descriptive spatial analyses and map visualization were performed in R using the ggplot2 package and a static bubble map template available online [25, 26]. The number of infants (n) and median SVI score for each state were summarized on both the county- and census tract-level. Bubble size represented the number of infants per state, while bubble colour represented the fixed SVI quartile in which the median SVI value for that state fell. Final nationwide maps were exported as high-resolution static images from R.

## Results

### Participant Characteristics

Two hundred fifty-six infants were included in this analysis (Table 1). Ninety-two percent of the infants were the result of a term birth (37 or greater weeks). One hundred twenty-seven (50%) were assigned female sex at birth, 78% reported white race and 20% reported Hispanic ethnicity. Infants were evenly distributed across the 4 geographic regions of the US, though 9% of the infants enrolled were classified as living in a rural area based on RUCA codes. Eight of the enrolled infants did not provide a mailing address and thus are not included in the data for this analysis. Despite the study title, ‘Infant Vaccine Biorepository,’ our study enrolled 23 of 256 reported receiving no vaccines in pregnancy, 20/256 reported no infant vaccines given in the first 12 months, and 12/256 (5%) infants had no reported maternal nor infant vaccination.

### Distribution of SVI

Based on nationwide census tract-level SVI rankings, 31.6% of infant participants were in the lowest social vulnerability quartile, 28.5% in the low-medium quartile, 19.9% in the medium-high quartile and 19.9% in the highest quartile (Table 2, left column). Based on nationwide county-level SVI rankings, 15.2% of infant participants were in the lowest quartile, 27.7% in the low-medium quartile, 24.2% in the medium-high quartile and 32.8% in the highest quartile (Table 2, right column). Maps were generated to illustrate the number of participants and average nationwide SVI rankings in each state based on participant census tracts (Figure 1) and county (Figure 2). Dark blue corresponds to the highest SVI quartile, and yellow corresponds to the lowest.

## Comment

### Principal Findings

Our infant recruitment methods have allowed us to reach infants from a range of geographic and socioeconomic backgrounds. The RUCA codes for our population suggest that most of our infants live in urban areas, while only 9% live in rural areas (Table 1). Based on nationwide census tract-level SVI rankings, 39.8% of infants in the study live in areas considered to be in the medium-high and high vulnerability category, and 60.2% are in the low and low-medium category (Table 2). Using state-level county SVI estimates indicated that even more (57%) infants fall within the medium-high and high vulnerability category.

### Innovation

#### Recruitment

Recruitment for clinical trials and observational studies has traditionally been done in person through connecting with providers or local flyering. Here, we recruit via an online recruitment platform that advertises the study on social media sites or through online searches.

#### Consent

Informed consent is usually obtained in person, where the investigator can adequately assess the participants’ understanding of the trial and ensure that the consent being obtained is truly informed [2]. However, since in-person consenting is often done at the academic, urban centre performing the study, it can create access barriers for individuals living far away or who face financial constraints. There are many options for remote consent. Here, we use REDCap E-consenting, which reduces the burden of travelling to a hospital while maintaining interactive, real-time communication with the participants.

#### Blood Collection

Participation in clinical trials often involves numerous in-person visits, sometimes just for blood draws or other specimen collections. The financial burden and scheduling constraints of in-person participation often mean individuals with low income, or those residing in high-SVI contexts, are less likely to participate. At-home blood collection reduces these opportunity costs and supports equitable participation.

### Strengths of Study

Despite the barriers in place that may have prevented families from joining the study, our remote recruitment and consenting methods made participation in the study more accessible. The use of SVI and RUCA as non-race/ethnicity metrics of social vulnerability is also a strength of the study. Most clinical trials publish limited demographic or socioeconomic data, making it challenging to understand the sociodemographic generalizability [4, 27]. Not only does our study report race and ethnicity, but we also report geographic location, rurality of the residence and social vulnerability as a closer estimation of socioeconomic status.

Using electronic gift cards as compensation via email, no social security number (SSN) was requested, reducing the barrier to participation by people who may be concerned about sharing their SSN or who do not have one. Many research studies in the US require a SSN to provide compensation for participants’ time, which limits who can participate [28]. Although our study is mainly focused on understanding vaccine effectiveness during pregnancy and in infants after birth, vaccination was not a requirement of this study, and some birthing parents and infants were not vaccinated (Table 3). Notably, 20 (8%) of our infants had no vaccinations reported (by their parent/guardian), 23 (9%) birthing parents did not report receiving a vaccine during pregnancy, and 15 (6%) reported never having received a COVID-19 vaccination. Our remote consent and sampling protocol was able to improve our outreach to medically relevant populations not always included in research, such as those who decline vaccination.

### Limitations of the Data

Although census tracts can provide a lot of information, using census tracts as a proxy for neighbourhoods, like addresses, may not be accurate on an individual level. The address at enrollment cannot represent mobility (moving to a different house or any experiencing housing instability) or capture specific experiences (likely culture, language). Furthermore, an address represents an area, not an individual, so some conclusions drawn from this data may not be entirely accurate in defining a participant’s experience, particularly for those who live in rural areas, which tend to be harder to classify and have more limited population data.

Another limitation of this analysis is that the most recent data on SVI is from 2022, so the SVI values may not reflect the vulnerability of today’s communities. As illustrated above, there is also a difference between SVI values when using census tract and county-level data. The counties are large geographic areas with populations in the millions and may inflate the vulnerability of certain residences, while census tracts reflect small communities that have a maximum population of 8000 individuals [23]. Once the census tract surpasses that number, the census tract splits into two new census tracts.

Although our cohort reflects substantial geographic and socioeconomic diversity, certain populations remain underrepresented. Recruitment advertisements (BuildClinical/Open Clinical) were available only in English, limiting participation among non-English–speaking families. In addition, enrollment required access to a smartphone to scan a QR code and submit interest, which may have excluded families with limited technology access.

## Discussion

When looking at the SVI and RUCA data for this study, it becomes clear that many of our study participants who are considered to live in highly vulnerable areas do not all live in remote or rural areas, but rather many live in urban centers. We are interested in continuing to widen the scope and reach of this study, particularly in rural areas of the US where there is less representation in vaccine research.

Since census tracts are smaller, more specific geographic units, the census tract SVI data is likely to be more representative of a participant’s vulnerability than county-based SVI data. Still, since we do not directly inquire about socioeconomic status (employment, insurance, or housing), we cannot draw definitive conclusions about the individual vulnerability of our individual participants. Furthermore, our race and ethnicity data show that our participants still do not match current US census data (Table 1). Although our sample does not represent the exact US distribution, it is more diverse than if we recruited from a single institution (or state).

Future steps include evaluating the diversity of vaccination history. Although we report vaccination status, we did not stratify the data by SVI or RUCA (Table 3). Understanding whether there is a relationship between SVI or RUCA and the likelihood to vaccinate could guide targeted public health interventions to improve vaccine uptake. We are also interested in evaluating participant proximity to healthcare centers. Some of the states represented in our cohort, such as Louisiana and Alaska, are among the most medically underserved in the country, particularly in terms of maternal and foetal health outcomes. As of 2024, half of Alaska’s counties were considered ‘maternity care deserts’, while Louisiana ranks 51st out of 52 states for preterm births [29, 30]. Our study design was able to capture data from infants living in some of the most medically underserved states in the country; however, future analyses are needed to identify whether our participants live in healthcare deserts.

## Conclusions

SVI and RUCA data show that the Infant Vaccine Biorepository recruitment methods have allowed us to include infants from a range of geographic and socioeconomic backgrounds. They also show that remote recruitment and sample collection can be particularly valuable for expanding representation in research studies. Equitable approaches to research should continue to be explored.
